title: Emile Christian and Anthony Sbarbaro Interview, 1959-02-11

blocks.x: I don't know.
There's a hell of a lot of them I don't read because that's what I said. I know. That's a French book.
Yeah, it's got a whole chapter.
Oh, by Gaufin.
It's got a whole chapter on there.
Who does he say that? I never take it.
He mentioned that you talked about Keppert, Perez, Vega.
No, no. There you go. I mean, that's what I mean. You see, none of them don't mention the white trumpet player. Vega? Vega was white.
You mentioned him.
Raymond Lopez, Christian. Yeah. They mentioned La Rocca. He couldn't even blow his goddamn nose.
And then they had Manuel. Well, Perez was a Mexican. What about Merritt? Mello. What about Merritt?
Merritt Brunas? They have good trouble.
How was Richard? What's Richard? Richard Brunas. Richie. Richie. Richie. Well, Richie didn't come up. He was in the straight. He used to play with fishers.
Well, who was the very first corner player you ever heard? That's a question.
Yeah, that you remember.
That you can think of.
The only good band in New Orleans in those days for an all-around band was Giordina. Which, Ernest Ottonio. Who?
Ernest Ottonio.
No, Ernest Jodtonio. They don't mention them in the book. I don't think you could pick up a book right now and find his name. It's in here. That he had the first good band.

But it's in French. It doesn't say that. Oh, I know him. I don't think it says that. I can't read French myself. Oh, it's in French, the book? Yeah, but it tells about, you're talking about Ernest Jodtonio and Tony Jodtonio both.

Well, Tony Jodtonio played with Emile's brother. I used to play with Ernest. I was playing with Ernest. He was playing with Ernest. He was playing trumpet and Edwards was playing trombone and back there was playing clarinet.
Well, let's start at the very beginning of your life. Where were you born? I was born right here in New Orleans. Exactly. Do you remember that address? No. Street?
The neighborhood of which part of town? No, I was born on Frenchman as far as I remember.
Downtown.
Yeah.
So you came up downtown in that neighborhood around Frenchman? What?
St. Claude and Rampart.
St. Claude and Rampart. And what year were you born? The exact date of your birth?
Exact date?
June of 27, 1897. I see.
Was your family musical by the way?
No.
Not a soul in your family played?

Not one. Not even a kazoo? Not even a kazoo. Didn't sing or anything? No. I doubt a very few families out of New Orleans had a family musical background. Maybe the Detroit's and the Christians. Well, the Brunesses might have had one at that time. Oh, yeah. The old man played violin. Well, not my family.

Yeah. But I have two sisters. Merritt and Henry, the ones used to play around more so than Richie. Richie used to play with Johnny Fisher when he used to play the parades and all that. It was more of a big band. They played 10 to 12 men in your band, you know.
Was Richie Stray?
Oh, was he a hard man? No, Richie was straight. Somebody told me he had a real powerful tone. You could hear him across the river. Oh, yeah. Yeah. He did have powerful tones. Yeah.

All the Brunesses had powerful tones. And the Varicella mentioned Henry Bruness on trombone. That's right. Well, he died pretty early, couldn't he? Yeah. Yeah, let me get you an act. Right here is an act. The Varicella mentioned Henry Bruness.
Yeah.
He and Edwards was the great trombone players of those days.
Well, how was Edwards on violin, by the way? Nothing changed.
He had to play good. I imagine playing a theater. Eddie was playing good violin. He must have played because I don't imagine he could play the theaters unless he could.
But you never heard him on violin?

No, I don't think I've ever been in a place where he played violin. I played with him in New York when he played violin. When after the band broke up, he organized his own big band. He used to play violin.

Yeah, he used to play with Bruno's band. Yeah, that was one of the few around. When they had sessions out there, they used to give the concerts, you know, at City Park. He used to play in those little stands, you know, with Bruno's band.

That's what I'm missing. In this carnival praise, that's why I think it's actually disgraceful. I mean, we used to have some good bands out there. Yeah, that's really, I heard something. What I heard in that parade, brother. The people used to go wild. The band used to take them off their feet. These people, they can't even put that double marching tempo.
They go faster, you can't.
Yeah, that's right. They're running.
Well, they ought to have the mules back, too.
Well, you see, when they had the mules.

They ought to have the mules and they ought to have the band. Years ago, every band was a hired musician. Today, these people, they pay some of these units, but not individually. Because it costs them money to bring them in. They know where you're looking. And why they don't, I'll never know.
You see, when we used to play the parades, we used to play five parades. We used to get $15 for the five parades.
There was no fooling around. A man went in and he got paid.

No, I don't know. Five parades, we used to get $15. Those are all the big ones like Rex and Conus. Yeah, all the carnival parades. They didn't, they didn't, they had the real. We'd go right out to the den right on Calliope Street there. And start from there. And go up to Louisiana Avenue, around, down St. Charles. Right around, the band's plant. And they had all the big bands.
I think I saw one union band in a parade here. I think it was a union band because they had white shirts on.
I saw one, too.
It sounded nothing like a band of years ago. Absolutely nothing. I mean, the people used to be yelling.
They had hot men in the street? Yeah, yeah. And what would they play? What kind of tunes?
Any, any, pick a tune. All that kind of stuff.
What was that?
All that kind of stuff. Tiger reg and all that. Used to play all that.
Take any number and play.
In the parades.
Robert E. Lee. Any, the march. Anything that was. That's where New Orleans. That's real New Orleans.
Would they take a waltz and put it in two? No.
No, no. No. Some marches. Some marches.
They would have too much mustard. They would have down home rag. That was out at that time.
Play all that. Go to those niggas out there in the front there. Those lights, you know, boys. He'd be strutting, you know. He needs to fight to get by band.
I heard a band in the parade here. Union band. I think it was absolutely. It was absolutely off. I don't know what it was. Because the rest of them were all kid bands, you know. School bands.

They don't have the same atmosphere like it used to have years ago. That's why you take a lot of the people. They don't go look at the parades no more. For that reason. Because there's no more atmosphere to it, you know. But before you get on Canal Street, you get up there, you couldn't move. You stayed where you were. You couldn't move. Because they had them jammed into the stores all the way up.

One, they cut out when they cut the picnics out at Millenburg, you know. They don't have no more of those type picnics, I don't imagine. No. That was real pleasure days, really good time days. And where can they go to there for pleasure? I don't know.
When did you play those parades, Mr. Christian? Oh, 1911, 1912. How long is it? 1910. When were you born? How old? I don't remember your birth date either. April 1895. April the 20th.
A couple of years older than Tony then.
63 years old.
I thought he was about 15 years old, but he was only a couple of years.
63. We used to bum together when we were kids. Yeah.
What's your real name now?
We want to get that.
My right name is Sparbaro. S-B-A-R-B-A-R-O. Sparbaro.
And where did this other name come from?
Well, the fellas in the band started calling me Sparbaro for shot.
That mean anything?
No, it doesn't mean a single thing. That doesn't mean, and it just stuck there.
It's no nickname, that's right.
What are your earliest musical memories of any kind of music or scene? What do you remember? What's the first thing you remember along that line?
I played with spasm bands down here like everybody else. I wouldn't dare mention their names or hurt their feelings, you know?
Yeah. Well, but what was the spasm band anyway?

A lousy band. Like, they got around here mostly today with exceptions of a few, you know? Mm-hmm. In other words, we used to call them, didn't call them bad, we called them spasm. They played with Jack Lane and all. Well, Jack Lane always had two bands.
Did they play with homemade instruments or like? No, no, no. Washboards or homemade. No, no, no, nothing like that. Just a real instrument, but you still don't know the spasm.
Yeah, well, Stale Bread, you know, had all those funny instruments he talks about.
Yeah, well, you couldn't call that musical instruments.
Yeah, yeah.

There has been instruments, I don't know if anybody's, like people trying to say that an African originated jazz. You go to Africa, even today, and show me one fellow that plays jazz. Show me one. They haven't got trumpets, trombones, and clarinets over there. They've had the... They talk about that because that... Of the drum, yeah. That's the most... How can a man in a book write a thing that an African, you know... Show me one even today, 1959, where a fellow over in Africa...
Well, they got some guys, but they're copying Armstrong or something over there now.

You know, it's going all the way back around to Africa instead of... Well, music over there is still getting bigger and bigger. Yeah. But I'm talking to being true when people say, where did they ever have a hot clarinet or a hot trombone over there? No, all that was all... If they did, they learned it from the... I'll tell you where they had hot trumpet players, nobody gives a lot of... Yeah. They had them some of these plantations in Cuba.
Mm-hmm.
Many, many years ago down at Victor. They used to go down there and pick them up right off the plantations.
At Victor?
Yeah, Victor had records out in about 1917.
Mm-hmm.

And they'd go down there, that's how they got the news. They had no newspapers. Mm-hmm. They had no radio. You know, they'd go down there and make a recording of the news and bring it around and play it, and people would listen to it. They'd know what's going on. Otherwise, they didn't know what was going on. I was going to hand them out.
Mm-hmm.
But I've heard records in Victor, you know. Mm-hmm. They weren't what you call cut clean like America, but they were more in the other jazz than anything you might hear in Africa, for God's sake.
Well, did those guys down in Cuba, would they have a dirty tone? Or would they just play?
Yeah, very dirty. Mud tone.
Yeah, mud tone. Would they play a lot of notes, or would they play good lead, or what?
No good lead. They'd just play their native music. Oh, yeah. And it would have a feeling of a good jazz beat. Yeah.
I didn't know whether they would play a straight lead tune, or how.
Oh, that's, that's, uh. The only place where they played straight lead tunes were in big cities. Mm-hmm. Those days. Yeah.

See, like, like over in England, you see over there? Mm-hmm. Well, when we first went over there, you had to play melody, see? Mm-hmm. The trumpet had to play melody. Mm-hmm. If they didn't hear the melody, they were out. They want to hear a melody, see? Then the others fill in around, but carry the melody. That's what they want to hear. As long as they hear that melody, they know what you're playing. But if they hear a lot of, uh, a lot of notes, they don't know what it's all about. They can't understand one thing from the other, see? So what they want to hear is melody. You play the melody, they know what you're playing, they enjoy it.
Well, what about a guy that's like that? Ray Lopez down here. Would he play straight melody, or would he be a get-off man, or what? Well, he would be a...

Oh, oh, that's... It was in between. He had his own style. Emil had his own style, and, uh, those days Johnny Detroit was around, he had his own style, and Brunus had his own style. Everybody had their particular style.

See, because everybody's feeling is not the same. See, you feel one way, this fella's got a different interpretation. I have a different interpretation. You have, he has. We all have different interpretations. You see, we get so far, we can do so much. But the other fella, you'll hear, he plays the same as you do, but he's got little different things that he puts in. Well, you listen to him, say, that's good. He listen to you, he say, gee, that's nice. And, you know, this one takes this, this one takes that, you know, and you put them all together, and with your own interpretation of the things, you make things out of them. You see? And that's how it comes. See, if we all had the same interpretation, it wouldn't be right.

Very few bands play alike, even down here right now. See? I was down the street the other night, no two of them sounded alike. Oh, by the way, who were the good drummers when you were here, huh? Right, Baby Stevens, Detroit, a fella by the name of Emil Stein. Emil Stein. You know, and Bob Stein. Johnny Stein. Well, Johnny Stein, but the real top drummers was Emil Stein. Emil Stein, he used to play. Detroit, yeah, and then the big. That was orchestra.
Stein played in the theater.
Yeah. They were capable of playing any place. In Detroit, too.
Now, what about in the streets? Would you have a good bass drum?
Oh, in the parades?
Yeah.
Oh, Jack Lane used to play bass drum in the parades, and other fellas. Tots? They had good, they had good.
What about Emil Gonzalez? Was he very good on the bass drum?
Never even heard of him.
Never heard of Emil Gonzalez?
No.
Johnny Lala was telling me about him.

Well, I mean, there's a lot of those names you see from those fellas. I mean, they get away from you, you know. Sometimes they're nicknames, too. Yeah, and a lot of times they get away from you from being so far back, you can't remember.
And Brown's, and the bands of those days that were known bands, Brown had what? What's his name? Billy Lambert on drums and the other fella?
Yeah, Billy Lambert on drums, George guitar.
No, but drummers, we're talking about drummers. Was Billy Lambert and who else?
There's Billy Lambert and then there's Freddie Williams.
Freddie Williams. Now, no, that was, he was in Fish's band, Freddie Williams.
No, no, no.
Brown's band? Yeah, he played with us. Those fellas all, you know. He went to Chicago. His brother Frank Christian had Tots.
Mm-hmm.
And Brunus had who? Well, the Brunus never had a band of their own pack they got at that time, did they?
No. No. Because, let's see. Henry used to play with, he used to play with Jack a lot, Jack Lane.
Well, Jack Lane, when he played a pair, he had to play his own drum. He was a drummer. You see, he was a drummer. His son was a drummer. Hansi. Both of them were drummers.
What about Angelo Sciro?
Angelo Sciro. Angelo Sciro. Angelo Sciro. Angelo Sciro. And clarinet. He used to play clarinet a lot. Angelo Sciro.

I wonder if he's related to Lukey Sciro. I forgot to ask Lukey. You know Lukey? Lukey plays in Buck Banville for years. Lefty Arm and they were all in a band. You don't know Lukey? He's younger. When you started on drums, is that your first instrument, was it, I understand?
Did you have a teacher, just pick it up yourself?
No, I wasn't taught until I got out of New Orleans.
What kind of a drum set did you get at first?
I got a real good set to start out with. I got a set that cost me those days $100, which was a lot of money for just two drums.
How old were you about?
Well, I left here in 1916. I left here. So I had to be 19 years old. I was under, before 19, because I was too young for the first draft. Too young for the first war.
When you first started beating drums, how old were you?

Well, I was playing in 1912, actually, making a dollar. In 1913, I got a little better. In 1914 and 1915, I was with Giordina. The reason I like Giordina's band is because, first of all, he could be independent. He had a good job, and he picked all good men that could teach me something. You understand? You play with a bad band, you're a young man to learn. Every man in his band was qualified. In fact, even these bands are today. Any of them down the street wouldn't play the rags that Giordina played that time. I proved that in New York. I brought some of those old rags, because my son's in the business, you see. And we chased them up some of the old orchestrations and put them on the stand. Those fellas actually had a...
They can't cut those standard high-class rags?

Is that the book you're talking about? They can cut them, but they don't do justice to them. It's the interpretation of it. It's like a fella, he can sing, but how does he sing? There's not too many opera singers. There's not too many, you know.
What about tempo at that time? How fast would you play a rags? Not like they're playing today.
Oh, slow stuff. Mostly slow stuff. I mean, nothing. Medium fox tracks. Did you play frog legs? Just medium fox tracks. You ever play frog legs? Blues and stuff like that. That's what they played.
Sure, we played many. We played, though. We were the only bands playing all of the rags. The only.
You know? Now, could you beat off the time? I say, would you remember about the tempo you'd play maple leaf rags?
That was fast. That was fast.

Not like today. Like a two-step or one-step, you see? They were playing almost half as fast as what they're playing now. And then they'd play the blues and then the medium tempos in between because people used to dance then. Dance. Not what they do now.

That ain't dancing. Well, even in spots today in New York and a lot of cities, they get a certain tempo, what they call a businessman's tempo, and they never change it. They just keep that same tempo for the people on the floor. Oh, I wanted to tell you, Joe Virgis works across the street.
Remember the guy who wrote Don't Leave Me, Daddy? Jesus. He works across the street at night. He might be there at night. Invictus.

I saw him last in New York so many years ago, whether he'll remember, I don't know. Oh, yeah. His song is in the same house where I song, so. Oh, yeah. And I saw him up there and I said, alas, I didn't know he was still around.
Yeah, well, if you check in tonight, if you're in the neighborhood, go across the street and ask for Joe.
He's an old man, too. Oh, yeah, Joe.
But he talks about you, you know, and the different guys and all that.
Because we used to feature those songs, Don't Leave Me, Daddy.

When we were down here, Joe was playing over on Rampart Street, I think. You know where Woolworths is now, Rampart and Canal? Yeah. Remember Tom Anderson's and all used to be, the cabaret. I worked in the Black Cat those days. He was playing around there in Tom Anderson's, I think, Joe Voyager. Because that's where the cabarets used to be, not Boyfriend Street. On Rampart and Iverville.
Joe's brother was a drummer, Louie, huh?
He had a brother, a drummer.
And did you know him?
No, I didn't know him. I knew of him, naturally. Yeah.
I think he was mostly in the theater.

But the piano player, I know, I'm trying to think of what, I worked in the Black Cat on Rampart, a couple of doors from Tom Anderson's. Because I remember we used to eat in Tom Anderson's late, you know, in the morning.
Did you know Charles Burgess?
By name?
I think he was a piano player.
I'll never forget Carl Randall, the fellow that played piano in the Black Cat. I'll never forget him.
Carl Randall.

He used to play with a racing form in front of him. We had about at least nine or ten singers in all different keys. In fact, New Orleans piano players, most of them couldn't even shine the fellow's shoes because he'd had to play in everybody's key. They'd feel hoarse. They didn't feel up to par. And he's reading the racing form while he's playing their song. I'll never forget him. Piano and drums we used to play there. He was a genius.
Yeah, that's what they had. Piano and drums.
I used to get a big $12 a week to play. Seven nights a week.
Well, how many bands in the, how many men in the Black Cat, I mean?
Two or three.
Two or three, huh?

That's all. I never had no big bands in there. There was only five men over the tracks in the real joint halls over there in the Tangle Palace. I worked there with Henry and Merritt Brunus. And I don't know who played piano. But I'll never forget that place over there. Remember Peg Leg?

Yeah, Anstead. Peggy Anstead. Yeah, an opera. I used to play for Merritt sometimes over there. They had a Jewish fellow piano player. Oh, really? I can't even place what was on. And they had Henry. Henry was playing trombone. I was playing cornet. And I think it was Eagle Beak Lamb that was on drums.
Eagle Beak, is that Billy?
Yeah, Billy.
I didn't know that.
Yeah, that's what I called him, Eagle Beak.
Was Vic Lubowski Jewish? Did you know him? He played with Tony Periniot for years. He was a piano player.
I play a lot with Tony up there.
Ask him about Vic. There was another Zimmerman who played piano. Roy Zimmerman? No, Tony, I think this guy's name was. And Roy told me they're no relation.

Then we had another boy who used to play piano over there with us too. From out of town. Every time we were ready to play, this guy was off of the stand. See? So off of the stand. Off of the stand all the time. So I said, God damn, I'm going to fix him up. So I got me some tacks. And I put them all around the piano stool. See? We started to play. Here he comes up running. Run! Get on the piano. Just tell me. Hey! Yeah, yeah. Yeah. But tax all over. I said, now you probably come up here on time.
Did you ever know Yellow Noon last?
Well, Yellow worked with the band in Chicago.
Oh, yeah?
Yeah, certainly. You work with him down here?
Oh, certainly. Sure. Yeah, we used to play picnics up there. Where would he play? He used to play with my brother too out there.
Where did you play with Yellow?
All the picnics and parades and everything.
Oh, yeah.
He used to really. Yellow was one of the stand.
I was wondering if, you know, they'd add a clarinet and a black cat or would they have any blowing up?
No, no. Yellow, as far as I know, didn't play in a cab right where I was. Oh, yeah. I doubt if he could play for the singers in those days.
Well, what about other violin players like Max Fink? Did they have many good ones other than there?
Oh, Giardino, but they had them around, but they wasn't using too many violins in jazz bands. We wouldn't get to know them. Max Fink was about the king in those days.
What was he the king in what respect? I mean, as a reader?
A reading man.
A reading man.
A little bit more finesse, I imagine, wasn't it? He wasn't. He wasn't on more jazz.
Today, it would be like the same old style. We wouldn't be wrecking, but I mean, then he was, you know.
Did you ever play many fights?
Oh, sure. Emile and I, we did most of them.
We used to go around the wagon.
Oh, yeah?

Yeah. Corner to corner. We'd get a fat big doll on a quarter for playing all over the place. And they had the fight ring on Bienville Street between Burgundy and the Tartridge's. Rampart Street there? New Orleans Athletic Club.

We played, the reason we played them, because Jardina had them, and he wouldn't play the fights because he was in the bank, you know. He had a good job. He was a cashier in those days. That was considered something. So, we would always have the job from Tartridge's and play in there and play the fight at night and receive that big doll on a quarter. But what was Tartridge? Promoter. He was a promoter, I see. He was the Madison Square Garden of New Orleans in those days.
Would you get on the street corner in Ballyhoo Farm?

Or would you get on the wagon? Only in the wagon. Not on the corner. Not at this corner. No. Go at the next corner. Well, there were some units. But if we go back to that same thing, Jardina, everything he touched was class. And he wouldn't have his men get off on a wagon and stand on a corner. Because I remember, you see, I've been coming out of New Orleans for some time, you know, every year or every two years. And I remember coming back here one time and seeing a band flat on a corner and pick up their drums and go on the next corner. Jardina wouldn't do that, you know. We'd be in a wagon advertising the fight, which is the proper way to do it, you know, because you see those signs, you know. You didn't have too much newspaper coverages then.

Then we had, we used to meet colored bands in wagons too, advertising the colored fights, you know. So we'd get on this corner, the colored band would be on that corner. That was some of the fun. We'd strike up, knock one out. We'd get through, they'd bust right and come right behind us. You know, we were following each other.
That doesn't exist down here anymore much. That was some of the things.
I've seen him on the wagon.
Remember Fasea, it was two or three years ago.
Oh, yeah, yeah. They were advertising, they were advertising the colored fights and we were advertising the white fights, you see.
Oh, well, this town is just missing the boat. They don't know what they're missing out. That's right.

Well, like they run those parades, that was enough, man. They have people running out under the wires. Big signs on the wagon. And what do they put those wires up there if they want to have the people standing on the street? Yeah. You know what I mean? They got the cables to keep them checked. I think it was absolutely disgraceful the way those things are run. Absolutely. People were under the... In fact, the fellas carrying the big lights couldn't even get by. Now could the archer. The band's playing things. Somebody in this town is far fast asleep and don't want to enforce them. I guarantee you one thing. They put a rope up in New York. They don't put a rope up. They put boards, you know, those things. Like you see the surge in water, you know. And when they put them, you better not crawl under one because they'll haul you right back. And that's the proper thing to do.
A famous fighter died the other day here. Joe Mandot. Joe Mandot?
We played this fight. I'll tell you who died just a couple of...

A color fighter. A mother by the name of Harry Wills. Yeah, he died. Yeah, he died just recently. His relative was working and she ran the ladies room in Nick's. She used to tell me all about it. I want to know if I knew him. I says, know him. I play these fights right here in New Orleans.

This goes to show you. I was coming up in a street call once. When the Claiborne street call used to run up Claiborne Avenue. I was coming up and I was just passing where they had the North's side fight arena back there. And I just get in around... Around... This is that street. St. Bernard. St. Bernard Broad. Broad and St. Bernard.
St. Bernard in Claiborne. St. Bernard.

Yeah. And then Harry Wills got on, you know. So I happened to say he was fighting rough house swears that night, see. So I happened to say to him, I said, well, Harry, how'd you make out tonight? He said, well... I tell you, he says, I'll win. He said, but that nigga sure is rough. He sure is rough. A rough house swears was his name.
He died with owning a lot of New York property up south. He did well.

He put his money in good juice up there. Yeah, they had... Then they had Harry Wills, the human scissors, boxcar shorty, rough house wares. Joe Mandot used to fight Johnny Dundee. Yeah, we saw a Mandot fight over here. Frankie Russell, Joe Thomas.
What's the little Pete Herman, the one that went blind? Yeah. They always have a lot of fights.
Did you play inside at the fights too?
Yeah, yeah.
Well what would you sit? Sit upstairs. We always had a good seat because
I knew upstairs. Music was a part of the fight.
They had a balcony like you know. Music was a part of the fight.
Would you play before or after? No wait in between rounds. In between rounds. Before two? Oh naturally before two. A minute in between 60 seconds. Something fast.

Something fast. Yeah yeah just something short. You know because a chorus a full chorus on any tune like any of your records is not supposed to run over a minute. No actually. So we played 40-50 minutes because once they started sounding that guy you couldn't interfere. Fast chorus that was it. Yeah and then in between when the fight was over.
In between the fight was over. And then we'd play a little bit the intermission you know.

You always played a few numbers before the fight started. Sure. And after that you know and when the fight was over you'd play a little exit march and that was it. Yeah but that used to be something. That was best uh one of the one of the main things of the fights today. It's the they're drawing out the monotonous. What they pay for the fight is that dollar and a quarter? Dollar and a quarter for the whole thing. The fight and the advertising. Yes. Everything. You'd make a lot of money. You'd have to advertise the fight in the wagon that day play the fight that night to receive a big buck and a quarter. I guess they knew the fellas wanted to see the fight too. Well you'd see the fight you'd have a you'd have a better seat than uh you know just as

as much as anyone. Well during that time everything was so cheap you know. Look when we used to go out to lake and play those picnics. Three o'clock. Nine o'clock in the morning till six o'clock in the evening.
Well you had your fun too. Yeah you had a lot of fun. If you had more fun those days what you're having now. Today it's money
and it's hard work. People used to pay a dollar and a half a couple to come in place. A dollar and a half a couple.
